newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia electoral changes fail to win support.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia electoral changes fail to win support.

text.p: A Slovenian referendum on Sunday failed to win enough support for changing the electoral system, according to first unofficial results, with voters showing little interest in the complex ballot.
None of three models for a reformed electoral system attracted the necessary 50 percent to be adopted, first results showed, and the referendum was therefore likely to be declared null and void.
About 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the referendum, which follows an inconclusive general election a month ago that gave neither right or left a mandate to govern.
Official figures showed turnout at 35 percent, compared with 73.7 percent at the end of the general election on November 10.

The option proposed by the centre-right Social Democrats -- a two-round majority system -- won most support with around 44 percent, according to first results. Under this model, a candidate would need to secure an absolute majority in two rounds of voting to win each of Slovenia's 88 voting districts.
Such a system was more likely to favour the bigger parties and produce a better chance of a clear result in a general election.

Initial results showed that acting Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats (LDS), Slovenia's strongest party, receiving 26 percent for their proposed system of proportional representation, in which each party would put up a list of 88 candidates.

The third choice on the ballot won 15 percent backing. This model, put forward by the National Council (lower house of parliament), combined the Social Democrat and LDS models, with half of the 88 candidates elected on the basis of a two-round run-off system and the rest by proportional representation.
Some 10 percent of votes were spoiled and about four percent voted against all three models.
The final official result will be announced on Thursday.
A commentator on Slovenian state television blamed the low turnout on failure to explain clearly to voters the differences between the election systems proposed.

Television said the referendum cost the country 400 million tolars ($2.8 million) just a month after 450 million tolars were spent on Slovenia's second general election since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.

An alliance of right-wing parties failed to win an absolute majority in the November election by just one seat. Talks between Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats, the alliance and smaller parties have gone on for the past month but show little immediate prospect of reaching an agreement to form a new coalition government.
